candidates.title: Why Will Starship Wait 22 Hours to Be Caught?
candidates.query: SpaceX Starship Flight 15 22 hours 14 orbits catch explanation November 13 2026
candidates.brief: Starship Flight 15 is designed to spend roughly 22 hours in orbit before the spacecraft returns, while the booster attempts an earlier catch. The video explains the mission sequence in plain English: orbital speed, reentry timing, heat shielding, propellant margins, and why the tower cannot simply catch both vehicles immediately.
candidates.evidence_summary: SpaceX’s Flight 15 mission description says Starship is intended to orbit at roughly 275 kilometers, complete about 14 orbits over more than 22 hours, and attempt a return-to-launch-site catch. The launch plan and timing are official mission details, not speculation.
candidates.science_angle: Orbital mechanics: once a vehicle reaches orbit, it is moving sideways at several kilometers per second, so returning requires carefully timed retrograde burns, atmospheric reentry, and thermal protection.

candidates.title: Why Waymo Tried to Pass the CHP Traffic Break
candidates.query: Waymo CHP traffic break I-280 San Francisco November 2026 explanation autonomous driving
candidates.brief: A viral video appears to show a driverless Waymo approaching and trying to navigate around CHP vehicles during a freeway traffic break. The video explains why this is difficult for an autonomous system: it must interpret temporary human instructions, blocked lanes, unusual vehicle positions, and uncertain right-of-way without a person making the judgment call.
candidates.evidence_summary: The San Francisco Chronicle reported that a Waymo appeared to approach and change lanes around CHP vehicles during an I-280 traffic break. The exact circumstances were unclear, and neither CHP nor Waymo had provided a definitive explanation at publication time, so the episode should be presented as an unresolved autonomy edge case—not proof that the system ignored police.
candidates.science_angle: Autonomous driving combines perception, prediction, mapping, and motion planning; temporary traffic-control patterns are difficult because they may contradict the vehicle’s normal lane rules and map data.
